transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-18 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Solutions), Samir Patel (CTO - ClearHealth), Dana Lopez (ML Eng), Marta Nguyen (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): Quick demo of Redwood Hosted API for chat and text; showed streaming, tuning temperature and max_tokens, and retry behavior. Customer asked about VPC/private deploy, SOC2, and retention. Next: share benchmarks and security docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, Priya will do most of the demo, Jordan here for any pricing ops.
[00:18] Samir: Thanks Alex, excited — we've been looking at hosted endpoints and want to understand how streaming works and what knobs we can tune for latency vs quality.
[00:30] Priya: Great, quick agenda, we'll cover the hosted API basics for chat/text, show streaming responses via SDK and curl, go over main params like temperature, top_p, max_tokens, then retries and some retry best practices. We'll end with a quick Console walkthrough for token accounting and Optimize suggestions.
[01:05] Dana: Sounds good — our main question is whether hosted will meet sub-200ms per-token for short replies, otherwise we might need dedicated.
[01:20] Priya: Totally understand. We'll show an example with small context length and streaming that keeps first token latency low; for absolute tail latency customers do pick Dedicated, but hosted covers many production use cases.
[01:45] Alex: Quick qualifier, Samir, what's your timeline and success criteria?
[01:52] Samir: Timeline is Q2 evaluation, want a pilot in April. Success criteria: average latency <300ms for 50-token responses, cost below $X/1M tokens, and SOC2-aligned handling of PHI.
[02:15] Priya: Good context. Ok demo. I'll open the SDK example — here's a simple node snippet. (screen share sound)
[02:30] Priya: Code: const res = await client.chat.create({ model: 'rw-chat-medium', messages: [{role: 'user', content: 'Summarize the patient note'}], temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 60, stream: true });
[02:50] Priya: When stream:true we get chunks back over an event stream, so you can start rendering the UI as tokens arrive. This reduces perceived latency.
[03:10] Dana: How are chunks sized? Is it token-by-token or chunked?
[03:20] Priya: Good question. It depends on model and encoder; often we send chunks every few tokens or 100ms depending on throughput. Under the hood we send delta events, and the SDK reassembles them. In practice you'll see small chunks so UI starts early.
[03:45] Samir: Any difference in cost for streaming?
[03:50] Alex: Cost is per-token generated, streaming doesn't change billing. But keep in mind prefix caching can reduce tokens needed if you have repeated prompts.
[04:05] Priya: Next, params: temperature controls randomness, 0-1 typical; top_p is nucleus sampling, top_k sometimes supported on some models, and max_tokens caps response length. We recommend 0.0-0.3 for deterministic responses, 0.7+ for creative generation.
[04:40] Priya: Here's a curl example for non-streaming: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -d '{"model":"rw-chat-medium","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What's new in cardiology?"}],"temperature":0.2,"max_tokens":80}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer ...'
[05:05] Dana: For retries—what's the recommended pattern? We have intermittent 429s and want backoff.
[05:12] Priya: We recommend exponential backoff with jitter. Typical is initial delay 200-500ms, multiply by 2 for each retry up to like 8s, and cap retries to 3-5 depending on idempotency. For chat generative calls not safe to blindly retry without tracking request id because you might get duplicate outputs; use idempotency keys when replays are possible, or do client-side merge strategies.
[05:45] Jordan: We also surface retryable vs non-retryable errors in the SDK and status codes for easier handling.
[06:00] Samir: What about streaming interruptions? If a connection drops mid-stream, is there a resume?
[06:10] Priya: Not a true resume on chunk offset today, but we make it easy to restart with same prompt and a deterministic seed or conversation history; for user-visible UX we recommend checkpointing the last received token and requesting continuation. We are exploring resume semantics in future releases.
[06:35] Dana: How does token accounting show in the Console?
[06:40] Priya: I'll jump to the Console. (switch screens) On the request trace you see tokens consumed: prompt tokens, response tokens, and the per-route cost breakdown. There's a token timeline and latency histogram. We can also set alerts for token or latency regressions.
[07:05] Samir: Nice. Can you show Optimize suggestions?
[07:10] Priya: Sure — Optimize will recommend batching, prompt rewrite suggestions, and quantization/model switches based on traffic. For example, if most responses are short it suggests lower max_tokens and a faster model profile.
[07:30] Samir: About models, are rw-chat-medium and rw-chat-small different quantization/latency profiles?
[07:36] Priya: Yes, medium gives better quality at slightly higher latency. Small is quantized and cheaper. You can set routing policies to prefer cheaper models for non-critical routes.
[08:00] Marta: Security question: where is data stored for hosted? Do you have options for retention and deletion?
[08:08] Alex: Hosted stores request logs in our control plane for X days by default; we offer retention controls and can disable storing full request bodies. For regulated data we recommend Dedicated or Private with customer-managed KMS. We have SOC2 reports and can sign DPA and BAA.
[08:35] Marta: Do you support customer-managed keys (HSM/KMS) for hosted?
[08:40] Priya: We support KMS for encryption at rest in Private and Dedicated; hosted has provider-managed keys by default but we have options in enterprise plans for KMS integration — I'll share the Security whitepaper with specifics.
[08:58] Dana: Any guidance on max concurrency per API key? We want to estimate throughput.
[09:05] Priya: It depends on plan. Hosted has per-account rate limits, and we expose suggested concurrency and we can provide baseline throughput numbers. For high concurrency, Dedicated gives guaranteed GPU pools and predictable throughput. We'll send a throughput spreadsheet.
[09:30] Alex: Quick demo of retry code snippet with backoff: // pseudo code retry up to 4 times with jitter...
[09:45] Priya: Also, for streaming we recommend keeping connection alive and using small chunk UI updates so you don't retry too aggressively on transient network blips.
[10:05] Samir: If we do a pilot, can Redwood run a small benchmark with our sample prompts?
[10:12] Alex: Yes — next step: you share sample request profile and latency targets and we'll run a benchmark on hosted and give numbers; if hosted meets it great, if not we scope Dedicated.
[10:25] Dana: About cost — is pricing per 1k tokens? Any extra costs for streaming?
[10:30] Jordan: Pricing is per-token for input and output, and for chat there's consolidated pricing. Streaming doesn't add extra charges. We have tiered discounts on committed usage.
[10:45] Priya: Now a live streaming example. (runs demo) You can see token chunks arriving, the UI updates as we stream.
[11:10] Dana: Looks smooth. Any SDKs for mobile/web that help handle partials?
[11:15] Priya: We have JavaScript/Swift/Kotlin SDKs and examples for event-sourced streaming; they include reassembly helpers and reconnection patterns. We'll share code samples.
[11:40] Samir: Can you talk about failure modes — like a partial generated output saved to DB, duplicated content, or double consumption?
[11:50] Priya: Right, duplicates are possible with retries. We recommend using request IDs and server-side dedupe logic, or client-side idempotency keys with a deterministic merge. For billing, tokens generated count even if connection drops — so monitor server-side acceptance.
[12:12] Samir: What about rate limit headers? Do you expose them?
[12:16] Priya: Yes, standard headers with remaining limits and reset times; SDK surfaces those.
[12:30] Marta: SOC2 — can you share scope?
[12:35] Alex: Our SOC2 covers control plane and hosted operations; we share the report under NDA. For Private/Dedicated, customers control more. We'll add that to next steps.
[12:55] Priya: Brief detour: talking about stop sequences and structured outputs — you can pass stop tokens to truncate outputs early which helps avoid extra tokens when you expect a delimiter.
[13:15] Dana: And function-calling or tool calls?
[13:20] Priya: We support structured outputs and tool/function calling workflows. For that pattern we recommend deterministic temp (0-0.2) and explicit schemas to avoid hallucination.
[13:45] Samir: Any limits on max_tokens?
[13:50] Priya: Models have model-specific context and response limits; e.g., medium supports up to 8k context, but response limit often smaller. We'll include model spec sheet.
[14:10] Jordan: We also have streaming vs non-streaming benchmarks in the workbook I'm linking here: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/clearhealth-pilot (note: placeholder)
[14:30] Dana: Great. Can you show the Console logs for a failed request?
[14:35] Priya: Yes — here's a trace: status 429, retry-after header, and the SDK log shows retry attempt 2 with jitter. You can export traces for further analysis.
[15:00] Samir: For pilot, if we need redaction or PII removal, do you provide tooling?
[15:08] Alex: We have pre-processing hooks and suggest client-side redaction; we can also integrate a redaction pipeline as part of the POC.
[15:30] Dana: Is there an SLA for hosted?
[15:35] Alex: Hosted has best-effort SLAs; Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets. Enterprise plans can negotiate SLOs.
[15:50] Priya: Quick note on routing policies — you can set route-level policies to prefer regional capacity or cheaper models, and set fallbacks. Useful if you want to failover to a lower-cost model under load.
[16:10] Samir: How do we track costs per feature?
[16:15] Priya: Console has per-route and per-token cost dashboards; you can tag API keys to attribute spend to teams or features.
[16:40] Jordan: We'll also provide an example JSON showing cost breakdown per route.
[16:55] Dana: Any limitations on request size for streaming?
[17:00] Priya: Large inputs are supported up to model context; streaming works primarily for responses. If you have very large prompts, consider chunking and summarization step.
[17:25] Samir: Are there examples of retries causing duplicate downstream side effects if function-calling is used?
[17:32] Priya: Yes, function-calling needs idempotency and careful design — recommend designing functions to be idempotent and use acknowledge/commit patterns on your side.
[17:55] Marta: Do you log user content in hosted? Is there option to opt-out?
[18:02] Alex: Default is to retain logs for X days; we have opt-out and data retention configuration for enterprise customers. We'll detail options in the security doc.
[18:30] Priya: Wrap up demo with a quick best-practices slide: optimize prompt shapes, set max_tokens conservative, prefer streaming UI, exponential backoff for retries, track per-route costs.
[18:55] Samir: Thank you — useful. Next steps?
[19:00] Alex: We'll send: pricing + hosted vs dedicated one-pager, Security whitepaper + SOC2 under NDA, benchmark spreadsheet and streaming SDK examples.
[19:12] Dana: We'll send sample prompts and expected traffic profile by end of week.
[19:20] Alex: Great. Anything else?
[19:25] Marta: One last Q: do you support SSO/SAML for Console?
[19:30] Priya: Yes SSO/SAML + SCIM provisioning and RBAC. We'll attach docs.
[19:40] Samir: Cool. Thanks everyone.
[19:45] Alex: Thanks all — we'll follow up on those artifacts.
[19:50] End of recording.
